analysis.title: GS TMT SPEC SALES: Pain in TMT; TSMC denies interest in memory; Nvidia idiosyncratic risk; Nexi block; A look at this week AFX, AMAT, VOD and more
key_insights: Desk view on 9 Nov 2026: investor willingness to take risk has fallen more than prices. Late-week conversations at hedge funds focused on protecting remaining P&L, cutting exposure and waiting for stability rather than buying dips. Many TMT funds are now down on the year despite the broader market. Index and factor hedges did not work last week.

Positioning and valuations have reset faster than confidence. Constructive investors cite strong underlying AI demand, protected near-term projects and scope for relief after extreme selling. Cautious investors cite unresolved funding and execution risks, few near-term catalysts, and reluctance to buy another false recovery.

Rotation debate: investors are moving into assets less exposed to AI (telcos, media, software including DSY, WPP, classifieds). Questions are now whether that rotation into safety is stretched, and whether some perceived safe havens carry longer-term AI risk.

SOX started the year at about 21x 2-year forward P/E and now sits at 10.9x, near the low end of its historical range and comparable to GFC-era troughs and 2013 semis downcycle lows. The only sustained lower multiple was the 2012-2014 trough (about 9-11x). Stabilisation of semis is seen as important because SOX led the market lower.

Memory names trade at low multiples versus semicap on 2-year forward price/sales: Hynix 1.9x and Samsung 2.3x versus ASML 17.7x and AMAT 14.7x. Constructive investors debate how much of an earnings downgrade is already priced in. DRAM names (MU, Hynix, Samsung) trade at 2-3x forward P/E while spot DRAM prices remain near highs.
NDX forward P/E is 18.4x, below the 5 and 10-year averages and the lowest since 2020.

AI concerns that built before the midterms: credit/funding and insufficient capital for the buildout (still the biggest risk, with CDS showing little improvement, which raises the stakes for neocloud reporting this week), power availability and permitting, cash burn, and returns on a growing investment base. The desk says the midterms added uncertainty on permitting costs and delivery timelines.

The desk says the situation is not evidence of an AI demand collapse. Slower capacity delivery could make existing compute more valuable while delaying revenue for equipment suppliers and new infrastructure projects. This helps explain the divergence between hyperscalers and spending beneficiaries. Constrained supply can still create inventory problems, cash-flow pressure and earnings risk down the chain.

TSMC denied a Friday report from The Information that it was considering making 3D DRAM at Nvidia's request. A spokesperson said it has no plans to enter memory manufacturing and remains a dedicated logic foundry.

Nvidia headline risk: CEO Jensen Huang reportedly admitted an affair with a woman reportedly identified as a suspected Chinese spy (per Bloomberg/Reuters). Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised and has launched a probe.

Datacentres: Google took over Crusoe's unfinished Wyoming data centre project, with plans to invest $17B in the campus. Microsoft is winding down an arrangement to rent AI compute from Oracle as part of a reassessment of cloud partnerships (Bloomberg).
ASML: Taiwanese DRAM makers are reportedly looking to buy EUV scanners to make DRAM on more advanced nodes. Nanya has announced plans and Winbond reportedly aims to bring EUV DRAM to market by 2030.

Nexi: Evergood H&F Lux sold 43.8m shares (3.7% of share capital) at EUR 4.50 via private placement after the European close on 6 Nov, cutting its stake to about 18.4%. The sale is GIC-managed Eiffel's entire indirect interest through Hellman & Friedman. H&F and affiliates did not sell their own shares.

Week ahead: OpenAI will hold an investor call on Q3 results after raising $11B at a $1.25T valuation (The Information). Reporting this week: IFX, AMAT, the two large listed neoclouds, and European telcos VOD, TEF and United. Wise could also be interesting.

Chinese AI models: no launches confirmed this week. Alibaba Qwen 4 is still in training, with speculation of mid-November. Baidu released ERNIE 5.5 Flash base on 5 Nov. Tencent launched Hy4 hosted API on 4 Nov.

IFX: stock about 30% below Oct highs. Buyside expectations for the 2027 AI revenue guide remain elevated (above EUR 4B). The desk thinks the stock may end the day up even on a disappointing guide, because hedge funds say they want to buy the dip.

AMAT: the bar is a beat and raise given peers, with the stock about 30% below Oct highs. Focus is on CY27 WFE trajectory, DRAM spending, advanced packaging (target of 70% revenue growth in CY26, BESI stake raised to 20%) and AGS growth into 2027.

Vodafone: numbers expected in line. Focus on KPIs, especially Germany given Deutsche Telekom's stronger broadband trends, and on cost cuts. An ECJ ruling risks invalidating Vodafone Germany's 2023 price hike. Drahi exiting his 50% stake in the OXG German fibre JV to Societe Generale raises the question of larger equity injections from VOD.

Desk recommends re-engaging via GS China Domestic AI basket (GSXACADO) after the correction, citing compressed valuations and domestic substitution momentum. Client activity in Asia shifted to downside protection via Taiwan Tech hedges (GSXATTXT, GSXATXTM) and short selling in Korea and Japan.

Oracle: meetings with the CEO and CFO were reassuring. Management sees minimal execution risk to the 7GW of capacity planned through May 2028 because projects are contracted and under construction, and expects AI demand to broaden into enterprise applications.

CrowdStrike: GIR sees the latest print as arguably the strongest in cyber. Revenue +26%, ARR +25%, record net-new ARR +51%, FY27 net-new ARR growth guidance raised to about 34%, Flex ARR +101%. The debate is valuation and execution rather than demand.

Derivatives: Thursday saw an extreme vol repricing after clients took off protection into Wednesday's post-midterm relief rally. The GS vol panic index hit 9.57 out of 10, the 3rd largest daily jump on record, following Wednesday's 4th largest drop. The two-day swing was the largest on record.

ETFs: US-listed ETFs printed $580B notional volume Thursday, the third largest day in the dataset, and 33% of the tape versus a 28% average. Friday morning ETFs were 36% of the tape with dollar volumes +65% versus the 20-day average.

GS Prime: global momentum down 4.6 SD and crowded shorts squeezing at +3.7 SD. Systematic L/S down 1.5% on the week, fourth straight down week, still +14.8% YTD. Fundamental L/S down 0.4%, +8.7% YTD. Fundamental TMT managers down almost 4% on the week, up only 1.3% YTD versus +25% mid-year. Info Tech and Industrials saw the largest net selling since COVID, and EM has been net sold 8 weeks straight.

US trading: market bounced Friday with semis up about 3.5%, which the desk calls healthy rather than a beta squeeze. Activity was quiet. Long-only funds were moderate net sellers on the week while hedge funds were net buyers, driven by Friday's cover bid in macro expressions.

UK property and autos: Savills issued a second housing market warning in a week after Rightmove cut guidance Friday. Used car values at BCA averaged GBP 7,244 in October, down GBP 73 (1.0%) from September.
